AI library guide

openvino-genai on Omarchy

Intel's C/C++ library for running LLMs locally on CPU, GPU, and NPU — no cloud, no per-token bill.

Reviewed 2026-11-05 · independent editorial guide

Short answer

Install with omarchy pkg add openvino-genai (about 2 minutes; 6.9 MB download / 21.6 MB installed). It's Intel's C/C++ library for running generative AI locally — LLMPipeline, vision-language, Whisper, TTS — on Intel CPU, GPU, and NPU. It's a library, not an app: you write a program that links it. Models must be converted to OpenVINO IR first (optimum-cli export openvino --weight-format int4). CPU works everywhere; GPU/NPU need Intel hardware plus drivers.

openvino-genai on Omarchy

openvino-genai is Intel’s C/C++ (and Python) library for running generative AI models — LLMs, vision-language models, image/video generation, Whisper, and text-to-speech — locally on Intel CPU, GPU, and NPU hardware, with no cloud and no per-token bill.

TL;DR

omarchy pkg add openvino-genai

Takes ~2 minutes. The store listing reports a 6.9 MB download / 21.6 MB installed. Apache-2.0 licensed open source, free forever, no paid tier, no account. Version 2026.4.1.0-1 at guide-draft time (store updated Oct 8, 2026). Project: openvinotoolkit/openvino.genai (614 stars, active since Oct 2023).

Read this first — it’s a library, not an app. There is no window to open, no CLI to launch, no config file. Installing gives you headers and a shared library (libopenvino_genai.so) that your own C/C++ programs link against. If you just want to chat with a local LLM without writing code, this is the wrong tool — use Ollama or LM Studio instead. If you want to build something that runs a local LLM, this is the tool.

Getting started (5 minutes)

1. The mental model.

OpenVINO GenAI sits on top of OpenVINO Runtime. You give it a model folder in OpenVINO IR format, pick a device ("CPU", "GPU", or "NPU"), and call generate(). The same code runs on any of the three devices — switching hardware is a one-word change. It bundles its own tokenizer (via openvino-tokenizers), so there are no extra dependencies to wire up. The pipelines it ships: LLMPipeline (text), VLMPipeline (vision-language), image/video diffusion pipelines, WhisperPipeline (speech-to-text), and text-to-speech — plus text embeddings and reranking for RAG. It also supports LoRA adapters (load several, blend them, switch per request) and optimizations like speculative decoding and KV-cache eviction.

2. Install it.

omarchy pkg add openvino-genai   # C/C++ headers + runtime library

That’s the Omarchy package. Two things to know: the package is the C/C++ runtime only (per the store description) — the Python bindings are a separate upstream install (pip install openvino-genai), and mixing the pip wheel with the system C++ runtime can break on version/ABI mismatch (see Common issues). Also note the Omarchy PKGBUILD builds upstream from source with a small Omarchy patch (linear-attention-guard-constructor.patch in the omarchy-pkgs repo).

3. Get a model (one-time, ~2 minutes).

GenAI does not run raw Hugging Face checkpoints — the model must first be converted to OpenVINO IR format. The standard tool is optimum-cli from Optimum Intel:

pip install optimum-intel
optimum-cli export openvino --model TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 \
  --weight-format int4 --trust-remote-code TinyLlama_1_1b_v1_ov

int4 quantization is the key move on a laptop: it shrinks the model ~4x so a 1.1B model runs comfortably on CPU. Bigger models (Llama 3, Phi, Qwen) work the same way — just swap the --model name. See the upstream Model Preparation Guide.

4. Your first program — C++ (the point of this package).

Straight from the upstream README:

#include "openvino/genai/llm_pipeline.hpp"

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    std::string models_path = argv[1];
    ov::genai::LLMPipeline pipe(models_path, "CPU");
    std::cout << pipe.generate("The Sun is yellow because",
                               ov::genai::max_new_tokens(100)) << '\n';
}

And the CMakeLists.txt to build it (C++17 required):

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.13)
project(genai_app)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

find_package(OpenVINO REQUIRED COMPONENTS Runtime)
find_package(openvino_genai QUIET)

add_executable(genai_app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(genai_app PRIVATE openvino::runtime)
if(openvino_genai_FOUND)
    target_link_libraries(genai_app PRIVATE openvino::genai)
endif()
cmake -B build && cmake --build build
./build/genai_app ./TinyLlama_1_1b_v1_ov

Same thing in Python (needs the pip package, not the Omarchy one — see the version warning below):

import openvino_genai as ov_genai
pipe = ov_genai.LLMPipeline("TinyLlama_1_1b_v1_ov", "CPU")  # "GPU" or "NPU" — same code
print(pipe.generate("What is OpenVINO?", max_new_tokens=100))

5. The three things everyone needs to know:

  • Intel hardware is the point; everything else is CPU-only. OpenVINO accelerates Intel CPUs, Intel Arc/iGPUs, and Intel NPUs (Core Ultra). On an AMD machine or a box with an NVIDIA card, GenAI still runs — but only on CPU, and the GPU/NPU options simply aren’t there. There is no CUDA path. If your Omarchy box is Intel, this library is the best-optimized local-inference option you have; if it isn’t, llama.cpp is the better fit.
  • The device string is the whole hardware story. "CPU", "GPU", "NPU" — that’s the API. But GPU and NPU only appear if the drivers are installed (see Common issues). CPU always works, and with int4 models it’s genuinely usable for 1–8B models on a modern laptop.
  • Version lockstep is not optional. OpenVINO GenAI, OpenVINO Runtime, and OpenVINO Tokenizers must match on major.minor.patch — only the revision may differ. Upgrading one without the others is the single most common way to break an install (see Common issues). The Omarchy package handles this for the C++ side by pinning its own dependencies; the moment you add a pip install into the mix, you’re managing it yourself.

Common issues & fixes

All items below come from the upstream install docs, the OpenVINO troubleshooting guide, or Intel’s troubleshooting pages — none are invented. None were reproduced on Omarchy.

ImportError: libopenvino.so.2430: cannot open shared object file (or similar missing-library error) after installing/upgrading

Documented version-mismatch failure. OpenVINO GenAI, OpenVINO, and OpenVINO Tokenizers must share the same major.minor.patch — only the revision may vary. It happens when you upgrade one package (e.g. pip install openvino --pre from the nightly index) without the others.

Fix: Pin all three to the same version, e.g. openvino-genai==2024.3.0 pulls openvino==2024.3.0 and openvino-tokenizers==2024.3.0 (install docs). If you installed the Omarchy package, prefer the system versions and don’t layer pip’s openvino on top. Unverified on Omarchy: the exact failure text with the Arch-packaged versions.

Link errors when building your C++ app — undefined references / ABI complaints — even though the headers are found

Documented ABI trap. PyPI wheels are built with _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0; upstream C++ archive distributions use _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1. Mixing the two ABIs is unsupported and fails at link time (install docs).

Fix: Practical rule: use either the Omarchy/system C++ install or the pip wheels for a given project — never both in one build. If you need a different dependency version than the prebuilt packages provide, the docs say to build GenAI from source instead. Unverified on Omarchy: which ABI value the Arch build uses — check before mixing.

available_devices returns only ['CPU'] — my Intel GPU isn’t detected

Documented in Intel’s troubleshooting: OpenVINO can’t see the GPU until the GPU firmware and driver are installed. Check first with python3 -c "from openvino import Core; print(Core().available_devices)". If GPU is missing, install the Intel GPU driver/firmware for your distro, and if it still doesn’t appear, set export OCL_ICD_VENDORS=/etc/OpenCL/vendors so the OpenCL loader finds Intel’s ICD (Intel troubleshooting). Also confirm the extra GPU configuration steps in the OpenVINO troubleshooting guide.

Fix: Unverified on Omarchy: whether Arch’s intel-compute-runtime / vulkan-intel packages are enough, or extra setup is needed.

LLMPipeline fails to load a model I downloaded from Hugging Face

You almost certainly pointed it at a raw checkpoint. GenAI loads OpenVINO IR folders (.xml + .bin), not safetensors/PyTorch weights. Convert first with optimum-cli export openvino --model <hf-id> --weight-format int4 <output-dir> (see step 3 above), then pass the output directory to the pipeline.

Fix: Second possible cause, per the OpenVINO troubleshooting guide: the OpenVINO version used to convert the model doesn’t match the runtime version running inference — re-export with a matching version.

NPU errors (PI_ERROR_UNINITIALIZED, -1102) or the NPU device won’t initialize

Two documented causes. First, the NPU needs its driver and firmware installed — without them the device simply isn’t there. Second, Intel’s own troubleshooting notes that IPEX workloads are incompatible with the NPU driver: if you installed the NPU driver packages and then hit -1102 from an IPEX workload, remove the NPU driver packages (intel-driver-compiler-npu, intel-fw-npu, intel-level-zero-npu) (Intel troubleshooting).

Fix: On a Core Ultra laptop, pick one stack per workload: OpenVINO GenAI for the NPU, or IPEX — not both at once. Unverified on Omarchy: NPU driver availability/packaging on Arch.

Pairs well with / If you hate this, try

Pairs well with

  • The openvino runtime itself (GenAI is built on it — likely pulled in as a dependency of this package, unverified), optimum-intel / optimum-cli via pip (the model-export tool — you can’t use GenAI without it), and huggingface-cli (for downloading base models to convert). For a full RAG setup, pair GenAI’s text-embedding and rerank pipelines with a vector store of your choice.

If you hate this, try

  • Ollama (if you want to use local LLMs, not build with them — one command, chat UI, model library, no code), llama.cpp (if you want a C++ inference engine that’s hardware-neutral and GGUF-native — the best choice on AMD/NVIDIA hardware), or ONNX Runtime GenAI (if you want a similar C++/Python library but with ONNX models and broader hardware: CUDA, DirectML, Qualcomm NPU).

Verdict: If you’re writing C++ on an Intel machine and want the most optimized local LLM inference with the least code, openvino-genai is the pick. If you have NVIDIA/AMD hardware, or you just want to chat with a model instead of coding against one, pick llama.cpp or Ollama instead.

openvino-genai is the free alternative to paid LLM APIs

openvino-genai is the free alternative to paid LLM APIs. Running TinyLlama/Qwen/Llama locally through GenAI costs $0 per token, forever, and nothing you type leaves your machine. What you give up: the frontier models (no GPT-5/Claude-class model runs locally on a laptop), hosted convenience (you convert models, manage versions, and supply your own hardware), and API ecosystem features (hosted fine-tuning, managed RAG). What you keep: private, offline, unlimited inference — and for small models on Intel hardware, surprisingly fast inference thanks to int4 quantization and the NPU.

How to switch from paid LLM APIs (~30 minutes)

  1. Export your model: pick the open model closest to what you were calling (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for a general chat API) and convert it with optimum-cli export openvino --weight-format int4.
  2. Swap the call: replace the API request with LLMPipeline(model_dir, "CPU").generate(prompt) — the prompt/response shape is yours to define, so keep your existing prompt templates.
  3. What doesn’t transfer: the hosted model’s exact behavior/quality, tool-use integrations built for a specific API, and usage-based billing (you trade it for a one-time hardware cost).
  4. Time estimate: ~30 minutes to first local generation, most of it model download + conversion.

Frequently asked questions

Does openvino-genai work on Omarchy?

It installs with omarchy pkg add openvino-genai and is built for Arch-based systems, but this guide’s steps were not run on Omarchy — see the verification checklist at the top. CPU inference should work on any x86_64 Omarchy machine; GPU/NPU need Intel hardware plus drivers.

Is openvino-genai free?

Yes. Apache-2.0 open source, maintained by Intel. No paid tier, no account, no telemetry mentioned. The models you run are separate — check each model’s own license (most open models on Hugging Face are permissively licensed, but verify before commercial use).

Do I need an Intel GPU or NPU to use it?

No. CPU works everywhere and is the default ("CPU"). GPU/NPU are speedups, not requirements — with int4-quantized models, a modern Intel CPU runs 1–8B models at usable speeds.

Can I use it on AMD or NVIDIA hardware?

Yes, but CPU-only — OpenVINO has no CUDA/ROCm path. On non-Intel hardware, llama.cpp will use your GPU and is usually the better choice.

Is this a chatbot app I can just open?

No — it’s a developer library. There is no GUI and no chat command. You write a program (C++, Python, or Node.js) that calls it. For a ready-to-use local chatbot, try Ollama.
